newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. persuading others to deny U.N. chief new term. [CORRECTED 16:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. persuading others to deny U.N. chief new term. [CORRECTED 16:00 GMT]

text.p: As the annual U.N. General Assembly debate draws to a close, the United States is convinced its campaign to block Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali's re-election is now being taken seriously.

The 73-year old Egyptian, the first secretary-general from the African continent, ends his five-year term on December 31 (corrects to make clear Boutros-Ghali is in his first five-year term). The 15-member Security Council must nominate a candidate for approval by the 185-member General Assembly.
The United States says Boutros-Ghali has not given enough attention to restructuring the world body and should go.

With Washington having vowed to use its veto in the Security Council against a second term for Boutros-Ghali, U.S. envoys say they are persuading member states that their opposition is not merely an election year campaign ploy.

"The private views we get from a lot of people differ dramatically from what we get in public," said a senior U.S. official, adding that presidents, prime ministers and foreign ministers talked of little else at the U.N. this month.

He said Washington was making progress in getting members to talk about procedure and set dates to discuss the election. Such talks are expected to begin at casual lunches, starting on October 14, and get down to substantive issues in November, after the U.S. presidential election.

So far, serious discussions in the Security Council have been rejected twice by members, with several saying they do not want to see the United Nations become a political football in the U.S. election campaign more than it has already.
One sign that encourages U.S. envoys is that less than half of the 125 high-level speakers in the General Assembly debate during the first two weeks publicly endorsed or praised Boutros-Ghali.

Aabout 22 nations called for Boutros-Ghali's re-election, most of them from Africa and the Middle East. More than 35 others, including Brazil, Paraguay, Bolivia, India, Indonesia, the Phillipines, Portugal and Greece, praised his performance.
Some diplomats, however, contend that Boutros-Ghali has received more public support than they had expected.
Among the permanent Security Council members with veto power, France, Russia and China have endorsed Boutros-Ghali in public statements, if not in the assembly. But Britain has remained silent.
If Boutros-Ghali cannot be re-elected for a second term, France, Russia and China are said to favor the idea of another African replacing him.

U.S. officials are painfully aware that any candidate the United States may prefer would be automatically rejected by many other nations, mainly because of the way Washington has treated Boutros-Ghali by first announcing its intention to veto his candidacy in the New York Times in June.

They say they are trying to end the impasse by convincing Africans to drop their endorsement of Boutros-Ghali and search for a new candidate or risk losing the post for Africa over the next five years.

Secretary of State Warren Christopher in his current trip to Africa, his first in four years, intends to make this point, particularly to officials of the Organization of African Unity in the Ethiopian capital of Addis Ababa.
"We are trying to encourage the Africans to come forward. There are several (names) who meet our interests," the U.S. official said without revealing who they were.

Among the African candidates mentioned are Kofi Annan of Ghana, U.N. undersecretary-general for peacekeeping; Salim A. Salim, chairman of the Organization of African Unity; Olara Otunnu, former Ugandan ambassador and head of New York-based International Peace Academy; and Hamid Algabid of Niger, the head of the Islamic Conference.

U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright has said the United States will insist on a secretary-general who is foremost an administrator and concentrates on reforming the world body, a definition not necessarily shared by other Council members.
The senior U.S. official said a new leader should have more of a "media presence" than the cerebral Boutros-Ghali and be able to deal with the public more easily.

"We do have a severe political problem domestically in getting congressional support for the United Nations," he said. "Someone who gets on television with a crisp statement about humanity or whatever the issue at hand...is going to make a huge difference in popular and congressional attitudes."
